title: Row over cash supply worsens as strikes loom
full_text:
Trust between the major banks and Armaguard has broken down, with the lenders urging the competition regulator to intervene and block the monopoly cash transporter's proposed pricing model, which they warn could lead to the national supply of cash running dry.
The Australian Banking Association told the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission on Friday that the Linfox-controlled company was trying to "charge a monopolistic price and impose unreasonable non-price terms" in proposed interim undertakings lodged with the regulator, as the long-running conflict between the two sides reignites.
The banks are also concerned by potential strikes by Armaguard drivers, after the company tied enterprise agreement negotiations to the finalisation of an independent pricing mechanism that would create a model for the long-term sustainability of the company.
Deloitte Access Economics completed work on the utility-style model in July last year and Armaguard said a year ago that it would accept it.
But an ACCC spokesperson said on Friday that the regulator had still not received a formal application for authorisation from Armaguard in relation to the IPM. Instead, Armaguard has proposed undertakings using a different pricing model.
The national secretary of the Transport Workers Union, Michael Kaine, said drivers would vote on Monday on whether to take protected industrial action as "workers can't wait any longer" for the issue to be resolved.
The ABA, on behalf of Commonwealth Bank, Westpac, National Australia Bank, ANZ, Coles, Woolworths, Wesfarmers and Australia Post, has been negotiating with the transporter for three years, to shore up its revenue as cash use plummets, so banknotes and coins can be delivered around the country Armaguard's major customers have provided $100 million in financial support over the past three years, which expired on June 30. The ABA said an offer to extend this support in August was rejected by Armaguard last month.
The ABA described the interim model, which Armaguard has proposed could operate for the next two years, as a "material departure from the good-faith efforts" to create a sustainable and transparent pricing model for the company, which continues to operate at a loss.
They also argue it is inconsistent with a new law that passed in August to give the ACCC and Reserve Bank of Australia powers over Armaguard, part of the trucking empire of billionaire and logistics magnate Lindsay Fox.
The heart of ABA concerns is Armaguard's proposal to adopt a "cost plus" model for new contracts, or those that expire, during the interim period.
This would allow Armaguard to form its own "subjective and unilateral view" on what costs are reasonable, the banks argue. It would then add a 10 per cent margin, which the ABA says is too high. The plan will reward the company for "incurring costs inefficiently" and allow it to make "take-it-or-leave-it" offers, especially in rural areas where alternative providers don't exist, the ABA said.
It also has concerns about allocation of costs under interparty agreements with other Linfox companies.
Armguard said the main purpose of the proposed undertaking was "to give customers confidence in the basis upon which Armaguard will continue to supply [cash in transit] services as the industry transitions to the new regulatory framework".
Armaguard chief executive Matt Caulfield said the cost-plus model would allow Armaguard to put current loss-making contracts onto a proper financial footing when they expire.
He said Armaguard would not charge any customer more during the interim period than would be allowed under the independent pricing model, while existing customers would continue to receive their current contracted price.
But the banks want the ACCC to make Armaguard offer customers whose contracts expire their previous contract price as of the end of last financial year, with increases of no more than CPI plus 7.5 per cent.
